detail:
Median arcuate ligament syndrome (MALS) is a rarely diagnosed and treated etiology of abdominal pain with no established diagnostic approach, according to a study in the Annals of Vascular Surgery. The researchers investigated whether their institution's protocol for identifying patients was effective, reviewing patients treated for MALS from 2001 to 2022. Under the protocol, patients were considered for a diagnosis of MALS if there was evidence of abdominal pain, unprovoked, provoked by eating, and by physical activity, together with celiac artery dynamic compression on diagnostic imaging.

A total of 163 patients were included. Patients who were part of the protocol had a higher rate of improvement in their abdominal pain (65.9% versus 50.0%), and patients diagnosed positive by the protocol experienced greater relief of abdominal pain compared to patients with a negative diagnosis (77.8% versus 52.5%). The authors conclude that, by using a standardized protocol, patients who received a positive diagnosis demonstrated symptomatic improvement, and that further investigation is warranted on a larger scale to assess its generalizability for this challenging patient population.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about median arcuate ligament syndrome research.
summary: An Annals of Vascular Surgery study of 163 patients describes median arcuate ligament syndrome as a rarely diagnosed cause of abdominal pain with no established diagnostic approach, and found that patients identified under a standardized institutional protocol had higher rates of abdominal pain improvement after surgery.
takeaways: mals has no established diagnostic approach, researchers state
a standardized workup protocol was linked to better surgical outcomes
larger studies are needed to test whether the protocol generalizes
research participation is optional; talk to your doctor about studies
title: MALS research: why patient selection decides outcomes
